content.text: {"relation":"DIVERGENT","consensus_summary":"All three blind responses converge on the same core: 'life/the life' symbolizes eternal, divine (zoe) life from God given in and through Jesus Christ, with Christ himself identified as 'the life' (John 14:6; 11:25; Col 3:4). Alternatives listed include biological life, resurrection life, abundant life, the Spirit as life-giver, and (in Response B) covenant flourishing through fidelity to God (Deut 30), but that last is treated as a secondary, largely OT register, not the meaning of the Johannine 'the life.'","book_summary":"The book defines 'life' as covenant existence — the life that the law produces — grounding this in Deut 30:19-20 and Lev 18:5 ('if a man do [my statutes], he shall live in them'), and applying this legal-covenantal reading even to John 14:6 and Matt 7:14. It explicitly flags the common teaching (Christ Himself, and eternal life imparted to believers) as the view it departs from.","consensus_core_identification":"Eternal/divine life in and through Christ; Christ himself as 'the life' — a spiritual, salvific existence given to believers, distinct from mere biological or law-based existence.","book_core_identification":"Covenant existence produced by keeping the law — life as the covenantal state of living in and by God's statutes (Lev 18:5; Deut 30:19-20).","core_relation":"CONTRADICTS","extension_relation":"PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION","boundary_disagreement":"The book keeps the same key texts (notably John 14:6) but reclassifies their referent: where the consensus reads 'the life' as eternal/divine life embodied in Christ and imparted to believers, the book reads it as covenant existence generated by the law. OT covenant-life texts (Deut 30, Lev 18:5) that the consensus treats as a secondary register become the controlling definition, and the christological 'eternal life imparted' sense is displaced.","material_contradiction":"The consensus holds that 'the life' is precisely eternal divine life in Christ, standardly contrasted in Christian teaching with life produced by law-keeping (e.g., Pauline law/life contrasts). The book asserts 'life' is the life the law produces, and its own common-view note acknowledges it is rejecting the standard identification (Christ Himself / eternal life imparted). Both cannot be the identification of the same term in the same sense: divine life given in Christ apart from law versus covenant existence produced by the law are competing referents.","rationale":"The book's core identification replaces, rather than sharpens, the consensus core. Response B lists 'covenant flourishing through fidelity to God' as a common alternative for OT usage, so the raw idea is not absent from the consensus space; but the book elevates that secondary register into the primary meaning and applies it to the very Johannine texts (John 14:6) that anchor the consensus christological/eternal-life reading, while explicitly marking the common teaching as what it departs from. That is replacement of the central referent with partial reclassification of shared cases, which fits DIVERGENT rather than REFINED (the consensus's central referent does not remain intact) or NOVEL (the covenant-law reading appears among listed alternatives).","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"One could argue REFINED: Response B explicitly lists covenant flourishing (Deut 30:15-20) as a common alternative, so the book merely promotes a recognized secondary sense; and the book might intend Christ as the true embodiment or fulfillment of covenant-law life, harmonizing rather than contradicting the christological reading. However, the book's own common-view note signals deliberate departure from 'Christ Himself / eternal life imparted,' and 'the life the law produces' inverts the consensus's law-versus-grace framing, so the contradiction is material.","confidence":"medium"}
